Vulnerabilities.Title: brotli: Out-of-Bounds Write in Google Brotli Decoder
Vulnerabilities.Description:
A buffer overflow vulnerability in the Brotli decoder (c/dec/decode.c) in Google Brotli versions 1.0.3 through 1.2.0 on all platforms allows a remote unauthenticated attacker to corrupt adjacent decoder state memory, disclose sensitive memory contents, cause a denial of service, or potentially execute arbitrary code using a crafted Brotli-compressed stream.





Users need to update any Brotli libraries or binaries between 1.0.3 through 1.2.0 to the latest available version: 1.0.10 or 1.1.1 or 1.2.1.

Vulnerabilities.Title: curl: curl: HTTP/2 upload Use-After-Free
Vulnerabilities.Description:
During an upload, curl mishandles HTTP/2 `RST_STREAM` received from the server
(with reason `HTTP_1_1_REQUIRED` or `REFUSED_STREAM`) leading to a use after
free of a `struct Curl_easy` object.

Vulnerabilities.Title: curl: curl: FTP wildcard write callback mixup
Vulnerabilities.Description:
When an FTP wildcard `LIST` operation fails, libcurl omits the restoration
path meant for successful listings, leaving the write callback set to the
internal listing parser and the write callback data pointing directly to the
easy handle. Subsequent reuse of this handle triggers an immediate crash, and
cloning it via `curl_easy_duphandle()` copies this corrupted state into the
duplicate. If the original handle is subsequently freed, executing a transfer
on the cloned handle causes a heap use-after-free read against the dangling
handle reference; alternatively, reusing the original or cloned handle while
changing only  `CURLOPT_WRITEDATA` (and omitting `CURLOPT_WRITEFUNCTION`)
results in type confusion, forcing the internal parser to interpret incoming
server response bytes into memory at the application-supplied write data
pointer.

Vulnerabilities.Title: curl: curl: info leak uploading over WebSockets with GnuTLS
Vulnerabilities.Description:
When curl is built with GnuTLS, a malicious WebSocket server can make curl
send memory past its send buffer. This is due to an out of bounds read
following when `gnutls_record_send()` returns a number of bytes sent **greater
than the number of bytes it was given to send**. GnuTLS does that after a
blocked send.

Vulnerabilities.Title: curl: curl: local interface connection reuse mixup
Vulnerabilities.Description:
When `CURLOPT_INTERFACE` (or the command line tool's `--interface` option) is
set with one of the documented prefixes (`if!`, `host!`, `ifhost!`), that
binding is not part of the connection reuse key, so a later transfer asking
for a different source can silently reuse an existing connection and go out
from the earlier transfer's source address

Vulnerabilities.Title: curl: curl: stale SigV4 headers sent unintended
Vulnerabilities.Description:
Setting `CURLOPT_AWS_SIGV4` to NULL but does not disable SigV4 authentication,
contrary to expectations and documentation. A subsequent transfer on the same
handle still sends an `Authorization: AWS4-HMAC-SHA256` header to whatever URL
isset next, leaking state information.

Vulnerabilities.Title: curl: curl: redirect to SFTP or SCP bypasses host verification
Vulnerabilities.Description:
A flaw in the curl command line tool's logic makes it only set SSH host
verification options when interacting directly using SFTP or SCP, and not as a
result of following a redirect.

Vulnerabilities.Title: curl: curl: FTP connection reuse inherits client-certificate
Vulnerabilities.Description:
An `ftp://` transfer configured with `CURLUSESSL_NONE` can reuse a pooled FTP
control connection that a previous easy handle upgraded with `STARTTLS` and
authenticated using a client certificate. The second handle performs neither a
new TLS handshake nor a new FTP login, so the server continues to authorize it
under the first handle's certificate identity.

Vulnerabilities.Title: curl: curl: server-set cookie erases cookie jar
Vulnerabilities.Description:
A remote HTTP server can set a cookie that curl accepts and writes to a
Netscape cookie jar but cannot reload. On the next invocation using the same
path for `--cookie` and `--cookie-jar`, curl fails before connecting, then the
cleanup procedure replaces the jar with an empty file, deleting cookies for
unrelated domains.

Vulnerabilities.Title: curl: curl: Negotiate credentials sent to redirected origin
Vulnerabilities.Description:
When using an *ambient user* in a first transfer doing Negotiate
authentication and asked to follow redirects, curl could pass on its
credential details to an unrelated second origin when asked to redirect there.

Vulnerabilities.Title: curl: curl: leaking host credentials to HTTP proxy
Vulnerabilities.Description:
An HTTP proxy can trick libcurl into sending the origin's credentials (Basic
password, or a Negotiate/Kerberos ticket) to the proxy itself, by answering
the `CONNECT` tunnel request with 401 `WWW-Authenticate:` instead of the
expected 407 `Proxy-Authenticate:`.

Vulnerabilities.Title: curl: curl: auto client cert connection reuse mixup
Vulnerabilities.Description:
libcurl's connection cache match function never considers the automatic client
certificate option, so a cached, already authenticated Schannel connection can
be handed to a transfer that got redirected to a different origin, even though
the code explicitly switched off the auto client cert option for that transfer
to prevent exactly this.

Vulnerabilities.Title: curl: curl: cross-origin reuse of a Negotiate connection
Vulnerabilities.Description:
When using ambient user credentials, an HTTP request directed to one origin
may be dispatched over a connection previously authenticated via Negotiate for
a different origin, leaving the request's intended credentials unused.

Vulnerabilities.Title: curl: curl: HSTS cache import drops longer-lived child
Vulnerabilities.Description:
Importing a `includeSubDomains` parent HSTS entry before a longer-lived child
entry, silently drops the child. Consequently, when the parent expires, the
child's valid HSTS policy is lost, causing curl to issue unencrypted HTTP
requests rather than upgrading to HTTPS.

Vulnerabilities.Title: curl: curl: Hsts Response Erases Persisted Entries
Vulnerabilities.Description:
An authenticated HTTPS origin can supply an HSTS `max-age` value that the
parser accepts, but time serialization later fails to process. On 64-bit
systems, extreme max-age values compute an absolute expiry within standard
time integer limits that exceeds calendar time structure bounds. During cache
saves, the original HSTS file is truncated before writing a temporary
replacement; when serialization fails, the temporary file is deleted, leaving
an empty or partial cache. Because the save error is silently ignored during
cleanup, curl exits successfully despite the data loss.

Vulnerabilities.Title: curl: IMAP APPEND plus CRLF conversion command injection
Vulnerabilities.Description:
Enabling `CURLOPT_CRLF` causes curl to advertise the raw input byte count in
the `IMAP APPEND {N}` literal while transmitting line-ending expanded data.
The server reads only $N$ bytes for the payload, causing the remaining
overflow bytes to be interpreted and executed as pipelined IMAP commands
within the authenticated session.

Vulnerabilities.Title: curl: curl: knownhost callback mismatches key as missing
Vulnerabilities.Description:
When libcurl uses libssh2 with a hashed `known_hosts` file, an unrelated
initial entry can cause host key validation to report a key *mismatch* as a
*missing* key to the `CURLOPT_SSH_KEYFUNCTION` callback.

Vulnerabilities.Title: curl: curl: wolfSSL public-key pinning bypass
Vulnerabilities.Description:
When built with wolfSSL, curl can successfully validate a pinned public key
hash against a key the TLS peer does not possess. During the TLS handshake,
wolfSSL validates the connection, but curl's subsequent re-parsing of the same
certificate - tricked by a manipulated validity length field - extracts and
matches a different embedded key, incorrectly authorizing the pinned public
key.

Vulnerabilities.Title: curl: curl: server-set cookie aborts cookie jar load
Vulnerabilities.Description:
When writing a long cookie name and value to a Netscape cookie jar, a remote
HTTP server can make `curl` write a record that exceeds its line-length
parsing limit. Consequently, any subsequent `curl` invocation reading from
that same cookie jar using `--cookie` silently aborts parsing prematurely upon
encountering the too long line, ignoring all subsequent valid cookies in the
file.

Vulnerabilities.Title: curl: curl: never-ending loop via server response omission
Vulnerabilities.Description:
By permanently omitting the final control-response line, a malicious FTP,
IMAP, POP3, or SMTP server can exploit libcurl and completely bypass its
configured transfer timeout mechanism, indefinitely blocking all concurrent
transfers bound to the same multi-handle.

Vulnerabilities.Title: curl: curl: TFTP direction confusion
Vulnerabilities.Description:
libcurl's TFTP state machine fails to validate state transitions against the
requested transfer direction, accepting opening server responses for both
reads and writes interchangeably. A malicious TFTP server can respond to a
download request in a way that forces the client into transmit mode, prompting
libcurl to consume and transmit data from the handle's persistent
`CURLOPT_READDATA` pointer - including data remaining from unrelated prior
operations, such as an HTTP POST request executed on a reused handle.

Vulnerabilities.Title: curl: curl: -J no-clobber guarantee bypassed with 103 early hints
Vulnerabilities.Description:
When invoked with `--remote-header-name` (`-J`), curl fails to preserve its
documented anti-clobbering protection if an intermediate 103 Early Hints
response precedes the final HTTP response, or if an `ETag` header is processed
before `Content-Disposition` under `--etag-save`. This flaw allows an HTTP(S)
server to overwrite an existing local file specified in the
`Content-Disposition` header despite the presence of the `-J` non-overwrite
constraint.

Vulnerabilities.Title: curl: curl: curl_mime_free stack overflow by recursion
Vulnerabilities.Description:
A deeply nested multipart MIME structure constructed via the public API causes
a stack overflow in libcurl during normal cleanup operations. An excessive
recursion depth within `curl_mime_free` leads to unbounded stack frame
allocation during structure traversal, ultimately crashing the host process.

Vulnerabilities.Title: curl: curl: Authorization: Negotiate sent to foreign origin
Vulnerabilities.Description:
When processing an HTTP redirect to a URL containing userinfo (a
`username:password` component), curl might erroneously retain and re-transmit
the original host's HTTP Negotiate authentication state. Consequently, a
malicious server can trigger a redirect containing arbitrary userinfo to force
curl to send a freshly minted Kerberos ticket—generated using the ambient
identity of the client process to an untrusted third-party host, effectively
bypassing the domain-scoping restrictions normally enforced by the absence of
`--location-trusted`.

Vulnerabilities.Title: curl: curl: password leak in CURLINFO_EFFECTIVE_URL
Vulnerabilities.Description:
libcurl could accidentally return a URL for `curl_easy_getinfo()`'s
`CURLINFO_EFFECTIVE_URL` option containing credentials, even though neither
the URL provided to libcurl nor the redirected URL did.

Versions prior to 1.1.1 use signed 32-bit arithmetic to calculate pixel offsets, allowing a crafted HEVC stream with large image dimensions to trigger an integer overflow and cause out-of-bounds heap reads or writes, potentially disclosing data, corrupting memory, or crashing the decoder. Vulnerabilities.Title: LangChain: MongoDBChatMessageHistory query injection can allow cross-session access
Vulnerabilities.Description: LangChain is a framework for building LLM-powered applications. Prior to 1.3.1, MongoDBChatMessageHistory does not enforce the documented string type for an untrusted structured session identifier at runtime, allowing the identifier to be interpreted as a MongoDB query condition rather than as a literal value when multiple users' histories are stored in a shared MongoDB collection. An attacker able to invoke chat-history operations can read, modify, or delete another user's stored conversation. Applications using authenticated, server-controlled string identifiers are not affected. This issue is fixed in version 1.3.1.

Vulnerabilities.Title: LangChain: RediSearch Filter Injection via Unescaped Tag/Text Values
Vulnerabilities.Description: LangChain is a framework for building LLM-powered applications. Prior to 1.1.1, @langchain/redis does not escape attacker-controlled values in structured RediSearch TAG filters and structured RediSearch TEXT filters, allowing injected RediSearch syntax to alter or broaden the generated search query. When an application uses an attacker-influenceable filter as a tenant or document-access boundary, the modified query can expose indexed documents outside the attacker's intended scope. This issue is fixed in version 1.1.1.

Vulnerabilities.Title: @modelcontextprotocol/sdk: @modelcontextprotocol/sdk: Unauthorized cross-session task access via taskStore
Vulnerabilities.Description: MCP TypeScript SDK is the official TypeScript SDK for Model Context Protocol servers and clients. From version 1.24.0 to before version 1.32.0, the experimental tasks feature (taskStore) did not check which session created a task. Vulnerabilities.Title: MCP TypeScript SDK: One HTTP request within the default size limit could exhaust server memory during validation
Vulnerabilities.Description:
### Summary
In affected versions, servers put no limit on how many array elements and object keys they validated in one request. One HTTP request within the default 4 MiB size limit could exhaust the server's memory, and the process aborted with `JavaScript heap out of memory`.

No credentials are needed, unless you authenticate requests before they reach the SDK.

### Am I affected?
Yes, if clients you do not fully trust can reach your server over HTTP. The risk is highest for `McpServer` tools whose input contains an array or a record. stdio-only servers are not affected.

Affected versions:

- `@modelcontextprotocol/sdk` 1.3.0 through 1.31.0
- `@modelcontextprotocol/server` 2.0.0 through 2.2.0

### Fix
Upgrade to:

- 1.x: `@modelcontextprotocol/sdk` 1.32.0 or later
- 2.x: `@modelcontextprotocol/server` 2.3.0 or later

**Upgrading alone changes nothing.** The patched versions add an `McpServer` option, `maxToolInputElements`, that is off by default. Make both of these changes:

1. Set `maxToolInputElements` just above the largest input your tools need, for example `new McpServer(info, { maxToolInputElements: 10_000 })`. It counts array elements and object keys in a call's arguments. A call over the limit gets an `isError: true` result.
2. Lower the request size limit to what your tools need. The option covers tool arguments only, and the size limit covers everything else. Set `maxRequestBodySize` on the transport or `createMcpHandler()`. If you parse the body yourself, for example with `express.json()` or Fastify, set that parser's limit.

If you cannot upgrade yet, make the second change. `maxRequestBodySize` needs `@modelcontextprotocol/sdk` 1.30.1 or `@modelcontextprotocol/server` 2.1.0. Below that, use a reverse proxy.

Vulnerabilities.Title: MCP TypeScript client SDK: HTTP client transports and OAuth requests followed cross-origin redirects and re-sent custom headers and request bodies
Vulnerabilities.Description:
### Summary
In affected versions, the SDK's HTTP client transports and OAuth requests followed redirects to any origin.

If an MCP server or authorization server redirected a request to another origin, that origin received custom request headers (such as an `X-API-Key` set in `requestInit.headers`) and the `mcp-session-id` header. On a `307` or `308` it also received the request body, including OAuth token requests with their `refresh_token` and `client_secret`.

On current runtimes `fetch` already drops the `Authorization` header across origins.

### Am I affected?
Yes, if your application uses `StreamableHTTPClientTransport`, `SSEClientTransport`, or the SDK's OAuth client functions such as `auth()`. stdio clients are not affected.

Affected versions:

- `@modelcontextprotocol/sdk` all versions through 1.31.0
- `@modelcontextprotocol/client` 2.0.0 through 2.2.0

### Fix
Upgrade to:

- 1.x: `@modelcontextprotocol/sdk` 1.32.0 or later
- 2.x: `@modelcontextprotocol/client` 2.3.0 or later

Redirects are now followed only within the same origin, and not at all in browsers. If your MCP server or authorization server redirects to another origin on purpose, configure the final URL instead. Setting `redirectPolicy: 'follow'` on a transport restores the old behaviour and the exposure.

If a redirect may have reached a host you do not control, rotate the API keys and `client_secret` your application held and revoke its tokens.

If you cannot upgrade yet, pass a `fetch` that refuses redirects, for example `(url, init) => fetch(url, { ...init, redirect: 'error' })`.

Vulnerabilities.Title: MCP TypeScript SDK: Server bearer authentication accepted tokens issued for another service
Vulnerabilities.Description:
### Summary
In affected versions, the SDK's server-side bearer authentication had no way to check that a token was issued for your server (its audience). Where one authorization server issues tokens for several services, a valid token for another service was also accepted by your MCP server.

### Am I affected?
Yes, if your HTTP server uses `requireBearerAuth()` or `verifyBearerToken()`, its authorization server also issues tokens for other services, and your `verifyAccessToken()` does not check the token's audience (`aud`) itself.

Affected versions:

- `@modelcontextprotocol/sdk` 1.6.0 through 1.31.0
- `@modelcontextprotocol/server` 2.0.0 through 2.2.0
- `@modelcontextprotocol/express` 2.0.0 through 2.0.1
- `@modelcontextprotocol/server-legacy` 2.0.0 through 2.3.0

### Fix
Upgrade to:

- 1.x: `@modelcontextprotocol/sdk` 1.32.0 or later
- 2.x: `@modelcontextprotocol/server` 2.3.0 or later, together with `@modelcontextprotocol/express` 2.0.2 or later if you use it
- `@modelcontextprotocol/server-legacy` 2.3.1 or later

**Upgrading alone changes nothing.** The patched versions add an `expectedResource` setting that is off by default. To turn the check on, make both of these changes together:

1. Pass the audience your authorization server puts in tokens for your server: `requireBearerAuth({ verifier, expectedResource: new URL('https://mcp.example.com/mcp') })`.
2. Return the token's audience from `verifyAccessToken()` as `AuthInfo.resource`, also a `URL`.

A token for another service then gets `401`. With only the first change, every request gets `401`.

If you cannot upgrade yet, reject any token whose `aud` does not include your server inside `verifyAccessToken()`. That closes the issue on every version.

Vulnerabilities.Title: MCP  TypeScript server SDK: Shared transport or server instances delivered one HTTP client's messages to another
Vulnerabilities.Description:
### Summary
In affected versions, an MCP server reached over HTTP could deliver one client's responses and notifications to another client. This happened when clients shared one stateless transport, or one `McpServer` or `Server` instance.

Messages were matched to a connection by JSON-RPC `id` alone. SDK clients number requests from 0, so ids collide in normal use.

### Am I affected?
Yes, if more than one client can reach your HTTP endpoint and your code creates the transport or the server once at startup, instead of once per request or per session. Until this release, the README examples of `@modelcontextprotocol/hono`, `express`, `fastify` and `node` showed that pattern.

Affected versions: `@modelcontextprotocol/server` 2.0.0 through 2.2.0.

Not affected:

- `createMcpHandler()` with a factory that builds a new server on every call
- stdio servers
- `@modelcontextprotocol/sdk` 1.26.0 and later

### Fix
Upgrade to `@modelcontextprotocol/server` 2.3.0 or later.

**You also need to change your code.** The SDK now refuses to be shared, so an affected app fails requests after upgrading: a second `connect()` rejects with `ALREADY_CONNECTED`, and a stateless transport rejects its second request.

Change to one of these:

- **`createMcpHandler()`:** pass a factory that builds a new `McpServer` on every call.
- **Per request:** build a new `McpServer` and a new transport inside the request handler.
- **Per session:** set `sessionIdGenerator` and keep one `McpServer` and one transport per session.

If you cannot upgrade yet, the same change fixes affected versions.

2. Return the token's audience from `verifyAccessToken()` as `AuthInfo.resource`, also a `URL`.

A token for another service then gets `401`. With only the first change, every request gets `401`.

If you cannot upgrade yet, reject any token whose `aud` does not include your server inside `verifyAccessToken()`. That closes the issue on every version.

Vulnerabilities.Title: simple-git: simple-git: `VISUAL` editor environment variable is omitted from unsafe editor detection
Vulnerabilities.Description: simple-git, an interface for running git commands in any node.js application, enables applications to execute Git operations from JavaScript. Prior to 2.0.1 of the argv-parser package, parseEnv omits VISUAL from GitEnvKeys, so prepareEnv drops the value before vulnerabilityCheck can classify it as allowUnsafeEditor. A consuming application that forwards attacker-influenced environment values can therefore allow Git to invoke an attacker-selected editor during operations such as commit amendment or interactive rebase when no higher-priority editor setting overrides VISUAL and Git's terminal prerequisites are met. The executable runs with the privileges of the Node.js process. This issue is fixed in argv-parser 2.0.1.

Vulnerabilities.Title: body-parser: body-parser: Denial of Service via unhandled decompression stream error
Vulnerabilities.Description: body-parser is body parsing middleware for Node.js and Express. In versions before 1.20.9 and in versions from 2.0.0 before 2.4.0, a single request can crash any application using body-parser with default options. When a request carries a Content-Encoding such as gzip, body-parser pipes it into a decompression stream and, after reading the body, leaves that stream with no error listener. A payload of one valid compressed frame followed by trailing bytes decodes and the application responds normally, but the trailing bytes then reach the already-finished decoder, which emits an error that is re-thrown as an uncaught exception and terminates the process. No matching route is required because body parsing runs before routing, so any endpoint that parses a body is affected. The issue is fixed in body-parser 2.4.0 and 1.20.9, and users should upgrade to one of those versions or later. As a workaround, disable request-body inflation (set the body-parser inflate option to false) so encoded requests are rejected before any decompression stream is created.

Vulnerabilities.Title: Element Plus Link component (el-link) implements insufficient input validation for the href attribute
Vulnerabilities.Description: Element Plus Link component (el-link) through 2.10.6 implements insufficient input validation for the href attribute, creating a security abstraction gap that obscures URL-based attack vectors. The component passes user-controlled href values directly to underlying anchor elements without protocol validation, URL sanitization, or security headers. This allows attackers to inject malicious URLs using dangerous protocols (javascript:, data:, file:) or redirect users to external malicious sites. While native HTML anchor elements present similar risks, UI component libraries bear additional responsibility for implementing security safeguards and providing clear risk documentation. The vulnerability enables XSS attacks, phishing campaigns, and open redirect exploits affecting applications that use Element Plus Link components with user-controlled or untrusted URL inputs.

Vulnerabilities.Title: fast-uri: fast-uri: Security policy bypass via improper host canonicalization
Vulnerabilities.Description: fast-uri is a dependency-free RFC 3986 URI parser and serializer for Node.js. In versions from 2.4.2 through 2.4.7, from 3.1.3 through 3.1.8, and from 4.0.1 through 4.2.2, for HTTP-family schemes the canonicalizeHost() function passes the parsed host to the WHATWG URL parser and adopts its hostname without checking that the parser consumed the entire input as a host, so the authority can be silently rewritten: data before an at-sign is dropped and tab, carriage-return, and line-feed characters are stripped, with no error reported. An application that enforces host-based policy such as denylists, loopback filtering, redirect validation, or outbound proxy routing on one representation can then see the canonical host diverge from what it checked, allowing traffic to be steered to an unintended destination. The issue is fixed in fast-uri 2.4.8, 3.1.9, and 4.2.3, and users should upgrade to one of these versions or later. As a workaround, reject an authority that contains more than one at-sign or any tab, carriage-return, or line-feed before calling fast-uri, or treat any non-empty parse error as fatal and compare hosts only from the same parse result.

Vulnerabilities.Title: fast-uri: fast-uri: Cross-Site Scripting via improper URI scheme decoding
Vulnerabilities.Description: fast-uri is a dependency-free RFC 3986 URI parser and serializer for Node.js. In versions before 2.4.8, from 3.0.0 through 3.1.8, and from 4.0.0 through 4.2.2, fast-uri percent-decodes the scheme component with the legacy global unescape() function before validating it, so an input whose decoded scheme is a dangerous token is emitted as a live scheme even though RFC 3986 does not allow percent-encoding in a scheme and no other parser accepts it. An application that screens dangerous schemes on the raw input and then stores or renders the normalized or resolved result can turn an inert string into an executable javascript, data, or vbscript URL, producing a stored or reflected cross-site scripting vector, and the equal() comparison treats an encoded and a plain scheme as the same, which can bypass equality-based allowlists. The issue is fixed in fast-uri 2.4.8, 3.1.9, and 4.2.3, and users should upgrade to one of these versions or later. As a workaround, reject input whose scheme part contains a percent sign, or check the parsed scheme against an allowlist after normalization and use that same parsed result rather than the raw string.

Vulnerabilities.Title: fast-uri: fast-uri: Path traversal via improper relative URI normalization
Vulnerabilities.Description: fast-uri is a dependency-free RFC 3986 URI parser and serializer for Node.js. In versions before 2.4.8, from 3.0.0 through 3.1.8, and from 4.0.0 through 4.2.2, the normalize() and serialize() functions apply RFC 3986 dot-segment removal to the path of a relative-path reference, even though that algorithm is defined only for the merged target path during resolution, so a leading parent-directory segment can be dropped and a document-relative reference can become root-relative. An application that normalizes an attacker-supplied or user-supplied relative reference and then resolves it, or uses it as a cache, deduplication, or authorization key, can have the reference escape its intended directory and point at a different resource. The issue is fixed in fast-uri 2.4.8, 3.1.9, and 4.2.3, and users should upgrade to one of these versions or later. As a workaround, resolve a relative reference against its absolute base first and normalize the absolute result instead of normalizing the reference beforehand.

Vulnerabilities.Title: fast-uri: fast-uri: Cross-site scripting via unescaped colon in relative URI paths
Vulnerabilities.Description: fast-uri is a dependency-free RFC 3986 URI parser and serializer for Node.js. In versions before 2.4.8, from 3.0.0 through 3.1.8, and from 4.0.0 through 4.2.2, when serialize(), normalize(), or resolve() are called with the non-default option reference set to suffix on a reference that has no authority, the emitted relative reference can contain a bare colon in its first path segment without escaping it, even though RFC 3986 forbids that because it makes the string reparse as an absolute URI with a scheme. An application that serializes or normalizes a relative reference with the suffix option and then treats the result as a URI can turn inert input into a live javascript, data, or vbscript URL, a cross-site scripting vector, and the equal() comparison can conflate a scheme-bearing reference with a relative one. Exposure is limited to applications using the non-default suffix reference option. The issue is fixed in fast-uri 2.4.8, 3.1.9, and 4.2.3, and users should upgrade to one of these versions or later. As a workaround, avoid the suffix reference option on untrusted input, or percent-encode a colon in the first path segment of the result before treating it as a URI.

Vulnerabilities.Title: follow-redirects: follow-redirects: Information disclosure via improper regular expression escaping in sensitive header filtering
Vulnerabilities.Description: follow-redirects is a Node.js HTTP and HTTPS client wrapper that automatically follows redirects. From 1.16.0 until 1.16.1, escapeRegex leaves valid header-name metacharacters unescaped in sensitiveHeaders. When an application declares a sensitive header whose name contains ^ or | and follows a cross-origin or HTTPS-to-HTTP redirect, unescaped regular-expression metacharacters prevent the generated filter from matching the declared header name, and the credential header is forwarded to an attacker-controlled redirect target. This issue is fixed in version 1.16.1.

Vulnerabilities.Title: follow-redirects: follow-redirects: Information disclosure via improper regular expression escaping in sensitive header filtering
Vulnerabilities.Description: follow-redirects is a Node.js HTTP and HTTPS client wrapper that automatically follows redirects. From 1.16.0 until 1.16.1, escapeRegex leaves valid header-name metacharacters unescaped in sensitiveHeaders. When an application declares a sensitive header whose name contains ^ or | and follows a cross-origin or HTTPS-to-HTTP redirect, unescaped regular-expression metacharacters prevent the generated filter from matching the declared header name, and the credential header is forwarded to an attacker-controlled redirect target. This issue is fixed in version 1.16.1.

Vulnerabilities.Title: follow-redirects: follow-redirects: Information disclosure via array-formatted headers during cross-origin redirects
Vulnerabilities.Description: follow-redirects is a Node.js HTTP and HTTPS client wrapper that automatically follows redirects. From version 1.16.0 to before version 1.16.1, follow-redirects removes sensitive credential headers (Authorization, Proxy-Authorization, Cookie, and any caller-declared sensitiveHeaders) before following a redirect that crosses to a different host or downgrades to a less secure protocol. The removal routine iterates the caller's headers container with for...in and matches header names against a filter. This assumes the headers container is a plain object keyed by header names. Node's underlying http.request, which follow-redirects is a drop-in replacement for, also accepts headers as an alternating array of names and values. For an array, for...in yields the numeric indices "0", "1", "2" and so on, which never match a header-name filter, so nothing is removed. An application that sends array-form headers and follows an attacker-controlled cross-origin redirect therefore forwards its Authorization, Cookie, and Proxy-Authorization headers verbatim to the attacker-controlled destination, with no error or warning. The sensitiveHeaders option added to fix CVE-2026-40895 / GHSA-r4q5-vmmm-2653 is equally ineffective, because it relies on the same helper. This is an unauthenticated confidentiality vulnerability: any remote server the victim application contacts can harvest the victim's credential headers by responding with a cross-origin redirect. This issue has been patched in version 1.16.1.

Vulnerabilities.Title: handlebars: Handlebars: JavaScript Injection via Own Property Check Bypass
Vulnerabilities.Description: Handlebars provides the power necessary to let users build semantic templates. From 3.0.0 until 4.7.10, Handlebars lookupProperty returns Function.prototype.constructor before applying the prototype-access deny list because constructor is an own property of Function.prototype. When an attacker can render a controlled template with allowProtoMethodsByDefault enabled and an accessible function in the template context, the template can traverse from that function through its prototype to Function.prototype and then obtain the Function constructor through the own-property bypass. This permits attacker-controlled JavaScript to execute with the server application's privileges. This issue is fixed in version 4.7.10.

Vulnerabilities.Title: handlebars: Handlebars: JavaScript Injection via AST Type Confusion in compile (Program.blockParams)
Vulnerabilities.Description: Handlebars provides the power necessary to let users build semantic templates. From 4.0.0 until 4.7.10, Handlebars.compile() and Handlebars.precompile() accept pre-parsed AST objects while validating only selected PathExpression, NumberLiteral, and BooleanLiteral values. This issue bypasses the AST validation introduced in version 4.7.9 for CVE-2026-33937. An attacker who can supply an object instead of a template string can place JavaScript expressions in unchecked values such as Program.blockParams.length, a non-PathExpression parameter depth, a non-string StringLiteral.value, or a non-string PathExpression.original. The compiler emits those values into generated JavaScript, causing code execution in the server process when compile output renders or wherever precompile output is loaded. Applications that pass only template strings are not affected. This issue is fixed in version 4.7.10.

Vulnerabilities.Title: handlebars: Handlebars: Cross-Site Scripting via unescaped closing script tags in precompiled templates
Vulnerabilities.Description: Handlebars provides the power necessary to let users build semantic templates. From 4.0.0 until 4.7.10, Handlebars.precompile() uses quotedString() in lib/handlebars/compiler/code-gen.js to emit static template text into generated JavaScript without escaping sequences that terminate an enclosing HTML script element. When an application precompiles attacker-controlled template text and embeds the generated source directly in an inline script element, a closing script delimiter can end the element and cause following attacker-controlled markup to be parsed and executed. Ordinary server-side rendering and precompiled templates served as external JavaScript files are not affected. This issue is fixed in version 4.7.10.

Vulnerabilities.Title: hono: hono: Information disclosure via malformed percent-encoded paths in serveStatic
Vulnerabilities.Description: Hono is a Web application framework that provides support for any JavaScript runtime. From 4.12.4 until 4.13.11, serveStatic can interpret a malformed percent-encoded path differently from upstream routing middleware and bypass protection for a static prefix. The root cause is serveStatic decodes a routed request path a second time before filesystem lookup. The attack mechanism is malformed percent encoding survives the first routing interpretation and becomes a protected path only during the later static-file decode. The affected component is serveStatic. The trigger conditions are an application protects a static prefix with upstream middleware and serveStatic receives an attacker-controlled malformed percent-encoded path. The impact is unauthorized disclosure of a static file that upstream middleware was intended to protect. The issue does not permit traversal outside the configured static root. This issue is fixed in version 4.13.11.

Vulnerabilities.Title: Hono: Query parser reads parameters after the URL fragment, causing cache-key and proxy interpretation differentials
Vulnerabilities.Description: Hono is a Web application framework that provides support for any JavaScript runtime. Prior to 4.13.5, Hono's query helpers treat a question mark after a literal hash fragment as the start of a query string, so the application can read request parameters that browsers, new URL(), reverse proxies, filtering rules, parameter allow and deny lists, access logging, request validation, and other middleware do not observe. The Cache Middleware removes the fragment when building its cache key, allowing a response influenced by parameters inside the fragment to be stored under a key that omits those parameters and later served to other users. This can bypass filtering and auditing, poison cached responses, and enable stored cross-site scripting when an affected parameter is reflected into cached HTML without escaping. Exploitation requires a runtime and intermediary path that passes a literal hash character through to the request URL; Cloudflare Workers and intermediaries that strip fragments are not affected. This issue is fixed in version 4.13.5.

Vulnerabilities.Title: Hono: Unbounded dot-notation nesting in `parseBody()` can cause memory exhaustion
Vulnerabilities.Description: Hono is a Web application framework that provides support for any JavaScript runtime. Prior to 4.13.5, when parseBody() expands dot-separated form field names into nested objects with dot-notation parsing enabled, it does not limit the nesting depth or the total number of intermediate objects created. Empty segments are preserved, so one deeply dotted field name can encode one nesting level per byte, while a large number of shallowly dotted fields can create the same amplification across a request. A request body within a normal size limit can therefore allocate an object graph far larger than the request after the body has already been accepted. An unauthenticated attacker who can reach an affected endpoint can send concurrent requests that exhaust the JavaScript heap, terminate the server process, and leave the service unavailable until restart. Dot-notation parsing is not enabled by default, and applications using the default behavior are not affected. This issue is fixed in version 4.13.5.

Vulnerabilities.Title: Hono: Incomplete fix for CVE-2026-39408: `toSSG()` still writes files outside the output directory
Vulnerabilities.Description: Hono is a Web application framework that provides support for any JavaScript runtime. From 4.12.12 until 4.13.5, the fix released for CVE-2026-39408 does not cover every traversal sequence, and toSSG() can still write files outside the configured output directory when a route parameter contains consecutive parent-directory segments. Static site generation builds each output path from the route path and values supplied through ssgParams, then verifies that the result stays inside the output directory using the same normalization routine that built the path. That routine does not fully collapse runs of consecutive parent-directory segments, allowing a path that the check accepts to resolve outside the output directory, and the check also treats output directories that differ in how they are rooted as equivalent. This arises when an application generates a static site from route parameter values it does not fully control, such as slugs from a CMS, API, or user submission. An untrusted ssgParams value can create or overwrite files elsewhere in the build environment and alter generated artifacts or deployment output. The vulnerability affects build-time static site generation only; request-time routing and applications with entirely developer-controlled ssgParams values are not affected. This issue is fixed in version 4.13.5.

Vulnerabilities.Title: hono: hono/jsx: Cross-Site Scripting via Unescaped Strings
Vulnerabilities.Description: hono before 4.13.7 fails to HTML-escape plain strings rendered by hono/jsx as a child or fallback of Suspense, as a string child of ErrorBoundary alongside an asynchronous sibling, as the single child of a Context.Provider, or as the root value passed to renderToString() or renderToReadableStream() from hono/jsx/dom/server. These paths stringify their input and treat the result as already-escaped markup, so an attacker who controls such a string during server-side rendering can inject arbitrary HTML and execute script under the application's origin.

Vulnerabilities.Title: ip-address: ip-address: Security boundary bypass via unclassified NAT64 local-use address range
Vulnerabilities.Description: ip-address is a library for parsing and manipulating IPv4 and IPv6 addresses in JavaScript. From 10.2.0 until 10.5.1, the Address6 isPrivate classifier in src/ipv6.ts does not recognize the NAT64 local-use range 64:ff9b:1::/48. Applications that combine isPrivate, isLoopback, and isLinkLocal for a trust-boundary decision can treat an internal IPv4 destination encoded through that range as external. Exploitation depends on a server network using an operator-selected NAT64 prefix within the local-use range. A successful bypass can cross the intended network trust boundary. This issue is fixed in version 10.5.1.

Vulnerabilities.Title: ip-address: ip-address: Denial of Service via unbounded IPv6 address parsing
Vulnerabilities.Description: ip-address is a library for parsing and manipulating IPv4 and IPv6 addresses in JavaScript. Prior to 10.7.1, the Address6 constructor, Address6.isValid, and parse code in src/ipv6.ts accept unbounded strings and expand invalid characters through RE_BAD_CHARACTERS into large diagnostics. Material impact occurs only when an application accepts a very large attacker-controlled field and passes it to Address6 parsing without an earlier length bound. Common URL and header limits, and common body-parser defaults, generally constrain the effect; common defaults typically exclude 32 MiB fields. Megabyte-scale fields can cause a synchronous stall and high transient memory use, approximately 16 MiB can trigger an invalid string length exception, and process termination occurs at approximately 32 MiB. The affected entry points include Address6.isValid and construction paths that reach parse. This issue is fixed in version 10.7.1.

Vulnerabilities.Title: ip-address: ip-address: Access control bypass via cross-family subnet comparison
Vulnerabilities.Description: ip-address is a library for parsing and manipulating IPv4 and IPv6 addresses in JavaScript. Prior to 10.7.1, the isInSubnet and isHostInSubnet methods in src/common.ts compare masked binary strings without validating that both operands use the same IP family. A cross-family containment check whose leading address bits match makes the masked strings compare equal even though IPv4 and IPv6 do not share an address space. An allowlist or denylist decision can therefore classify an address outside the intended range as contained. This issue is fixed in version 10.7.1.

Vulnerabilities.Title: ip-address: ip-address: Security bypass via incomplete IPv6 link-local address validation
Vulnerabilities.Description: ip-address is a library for parsing and manipulating IPv4 and IPv6 addresses in JavaScript. Prior to 10.5.1, the Address6 isLinkLocal method in src/ipv6.ts recognizes only fe80::/64 instead of the complete fe80::/10 IPv6 link-local range. An attacker-controlled address elsewhere in fe80::/10 can therefore pass a trust-boundary check that relies on isLinkLocal. The same address is identified as link-local by getType and getScope, exposing the inconsistent classification. A successful bypass can reach an on-link host outside the intended trust boundary. This issue is fixed in version 10.5.1.

Vulnerabilities.Title: ip-address: ip-address: Denial of Service via excessive percent characters in IPv6 address input
Vulnerabilities.Description: ip-address before 10.7.4 allows a denial of service (CPU consumption from quadratic complexity, and application stall) via many % characters in input reaching a function call that uses the Address6 constructor.

Vulnerabilities.Title: markdown-it: markdown-it: Denial of Service via mismatched quote parsing
Vulnerabilities.Description: markdown-it is a Markdown parser. Prior to 14.3.2 and 15.0.2, when typographer: true is enabled, specially crafted Markdown can cause quadratic processing time in the smartquotes rule, potentially leading to denial of service in applications processing untrusted input. Many opening double quotes followed by unmatched closing single quotes cause repeated scans of the entire opener stack. The same issue occurs with the quote types reversed. The default configuration (typographer: false) is not affected, but this option is enabled with high probability. This issue is fixed in versions 14.3.2 and 15.0.2.

Vulnerabilities.Title: markdown-it: markdown-it: Denial of Service via Regular Expression Denial of Service in linkify function
Vulnerabilities.Description: Versions of the package markdown-it from 13.0.0 and before 14.1.1 are vulnerable to Regular Expression Denial of Service (ReDoS) due to the use of the regex /\*+$/ in the linkify function. An attacker can supply a long sequence of * characters followed by a non-matching character, which triggers excessive backtracking and may lead to a denial-of-service condition.

Vulnerabilities.Title: markdown-it: markdown-it: Denial of Service via quadratic processing of smartquotes with typographer enabled
Vulnerabilities.Description: markdown-it is a Markdown parser. Versions 14.1.1 and below contain a denial-of-service vulnerability when typographer: true is enabled, due to quadratic (O(n^2)) processing in the smartquotes rule. The issue stems from repeatedly modifying strings with replaceAt(), which performs O(n) slicing and concatenation per quote character. This can cause excessive CPU consumption when parsing quote-heavy, user-supplied markdown and may let attackers degrade or disrupt service availability. Although typographer is disabled by default, many production apps enable it for smart typography, making the issue relevant. This issue has been fixed in version 14.2.0.

Vulnerabilities.Title: markdown-it linkify: true has two quadratic paths, so a few hundred KB of markdown blocks the event loop for tens of seconds
Vulnerabilities.Description:
## Summary

Two independent quadratic paths in the `linkify: true` handling. Both are in markdown-it's own code rather than in linkify-it, which stays linear on both payloads.

`src/rules_core/linkify.ts` calls `arrayReplaceAt` once per linkified text token, and that rebuilds the whole `children` array each time. A paragraph of N soft-broken lines is one inline token with about 2N children, so you get N rebuilds over a 2N array. Schema-less emails are what reach it. A `http://` link gets consumed by the inline rule first and never arrives as a text token, so those stay linear.

`src/rules_inline/linkify.ts` runs `state.pending.match(SCHEME_RE)` at every `://` in the source. `state.pending` only gets truncated once a link is actually produced, so an unregistered scheme leaves it growing and every `://` rescans the lot.

## Proof of concept

Clean install of 15.0.0 from npm, `new MarkdownIt({ linkify: true }).render(payload)`, Node 24.

| N | 5,000 | 10,000 | 20,000 | 40,000 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `'a@b.co\n'.repeat(N)`, 34KB to 273KB | 1.1s | 4.7s | 19.6s | 89s |
| `'a://'.repeat(N)`, 20KB to 156KB | 0.25s | 0.76s | 3.1s | 15.0s |

Doubling the input roughly quadruples the time in both. With `linkify: false` the same inputs run in 25 to 131ms and stay flat.

Controls for the first one, all at N=20000: putting every email in a single text token (`'a@b.co '`) takes 0.59s, one email per paragraph (`'a@b.co\n\n'`) takes 0.64s, and soft-broken lines with nothing linkifiable take 42ms. So it needs many children AND many of them linkifying. For the second, replaying just the `SCHEME_RE` calls against the same growing prefixes with no markdown-it involved accounts for 11.7s of the 15s.

Ordinary prose does it too. `'ping a@b.co ok\n'.repeat(20000)` is 293KB and takes 31s.

## Caveat

`linkify` is off by default, so this only reaches apps that turn it on.

## Impact

Availability only. A few hundred KB of fairly ordinary markdown pins one core for tens of seconds, and because it's quadratic it degrades quickly with size. Nothing is read, written or executed.

Vulnerabilities.Title: markdown-it: markdown-it: Denial of Service via repeated unterminated inline HTML constructs
Vulnerabilities.Description: markdown-it is a Markdown parser. Prior to 14.3.3 and 15.0.3, when the html option or commonmark preset is enabled and the constructs occur inside a paragraph, attacker-controlled Markdown containing repeated unterminated inline HTML comments, processing instructions, declarations, or CDATA sections reaches src/rules_inline/html_inline.ts. Its HTML_TAG_RE match searches the remaining suffix for the appropriate terminator; when no terminator is present, parsing advances to the next opener and repeats the match over overlapping input, causing quadratic processing and denial of service through event-loop blocking or an unresponsive browser main thread. HTML blocks and the default HTML-disabled configuration are not affected by these payloads. This issue is fixed in versions 14.3.3 and 15.0.3.

Vulnerabilities.Title: moment: Moment: Path Traversal via crafted non-string input to locale function
Vulnerabilities.Description: moment is a JavaScript date library for parsing, validating, manipulating, and formatting dates. In versions 2.29.2 through 2.30.1, a specially crafted non-string object passed to moment.locale() can bypass the locale-name path-traversal guard. The guard assumes the input is a string, so an object whose match() method satisfies the check while its toString() returns a traversal path reaches an internal require() call with attacker-controlled path segments. This is an incomplete fix for CVE-2022-24785 and primarily affects npm (server-side) users that pass user-provided input directly to moment.locale(). The issue is fixed in moment 2.31.0, and users should upgrade to 2.31.0 or later. As a workaround, validate that any user-supplied input is a string before passing it to moment.locale().

Vulnerabilities.Title: multer: multer: Denial of Service via aborted request during asynchronous file filtering
Vulnerabilities.Description: multer is a middleware for Node.js that handles multipart/form-data file uploads. In versions from 2.0.0 before 2.5.0, when multer is configured with an asynchronous fileFilter, a single request can crash the Node.js process. If the request is aborted while one file's asynchronous fileFilter is still pending, the pending callback later resumes a parsing stream that multer has already torn down, and the underlying parser emits an error on a stream that no longer has an error listener, which Node raises as an unhandled error event so the process exits. Any application using multer with an asynchronous fileFilter is affected regardless of storage engine, while uploads using a synchronous fileFilter are not affected. The issue is fixed in multer 2.5.0, and users should upgrade to 2.5.0 or later. As a workaround, use a synchronous fileFilter.

Vulnerabilities.Title: multer: multer: Denial of Service via orphaned disk writes on aborted uploads
Vulnerabilities.Description: multer is a Node.js middleware for handling multipart/form-data uploads. In versions 2.2.0 through 2.3.0, when a request using disk storage is aborted mid-upload, file writes that complete after multer has already run its abort cleanup are not removed, so each aborted upload can leave an orphaned file on disk. A remote unauthenticated attacker can repeatedly start and abort uploads to accumulate orphaned files and exhaust disk space, causing a denial of service. The issue is fixed in multer 2.4.0, and users should upgrade to 2.4.0 or later.

Vulnerabilities.Title: nodemailer: Nodemailer: Arbitrary file read and Server-Side Request Forgery via raw option bypass
Vulnerabilities.Description: nodemailer before 9.0.1 fails to apply disableFileAccess and disableUrlAccess flags to message-level raw option, allowing authenticated attackers to read arbitrary files or perform server-side request forgery by supplying path or href properties. Attackers can exploit this by crafting raw messages with file paths or URLs that bypass the intended sandbox, with fetched content delivered in the outgoing message to attacker-controlled recipients.

Vulnerabilities.Title: Nodemailer: Quadratic (O(n²)) time complexity in addressparser allows remote denial of service via a crafted address list
Vulnerabilities.Description:
### Summary

Nodemailer's address parser (`lib/addressparser/index.js`) parses a list of comma‑separated addresses in **quadratic time — O(n²)** in the number of addresses. A single crafted address string (e.g. a `To`, `Cc`, `Bcc`, `From`, or `Reply‑To` value, or any value passed to the exported `addressparser`) therefore consumes CPU proportional to the **square** of its length and blocks Node's single‑threaded event loop for the entire duration, denying service to every other request in the process.

This requires **no special application configuration and no cooperating receiver** — it is entirely inside the parser and triggers on the library's default code path. A ~1.5 MB address value freezes the process for ~25–30 seconds of 100% CPU; the cost grows with the square of the input, so a few‑MB value stalls the server for minutes. It is a distinct issue from the recursion DoS fixed as CVE‑2025‑14874 (that path is guarded by a nesting‑depth cap; this one is a flat, comma‑separated list with no such limit).

### Details

`addressparser` tokenizes the input, splits it into per‑address token groups, and then accumulates the parsed results in a loop (`lib/addressparser/index.js`, ~lines 500–505):

```js
addresses.forEach(addr => {
    const handled = _handleAddress(addr, depth);
    if (handled.length) {
        parsedAddresses = parsedAddresses.concat(handled);   // <-- line ~503
    }
});
```

`Array.prototype.concat` builds and returns a **new** array containing a copy of every element accumulated so far. Reassigning `parsedAddresses = parsedAddresses.concat(handled)` on each of the *n* iterations copies 1 + 2 + 3 + … + n elements in total, i.e. **O(n²)** work (and O(n²) transient allocations) for an input containing *n* addresses. Tokenization and `_handleAddress` themselves are linear; the quadratic blowup is entirely this accumulator.

**Root‑cause proof.** Replacing only that line with an in‑place append and re‑running the exact same input:

```
parsedAddresses = parsedAddresses.concat(handled);      ->  100000 addresses:  ~6068 ms
parsedAddresses.push.apply(parsedAddresses, handled);   ->  100000 addresses:  ~51 ms   (≈119x faster, now linear)
```

**Measured scaling** (nodemailer 9.0.6, `'a@b.com,'.repeat(n)`):

| addresses n | input size | parse time | ratio for 2× input |
|---|---|---|---|
| 25,000  | 0.19 MB | ~0.35 s | – |
| 50,000  | 0.38 MB | ~1.4 s  | ×4.0 |
| 100,000 | 0.76 MB | ~6–8 s  | ×3.9 |
| 200,000 | 1.53 MB | ~25–30 s| ×4.1 |

Doubling the input quadruples the time — the signature of O(n²).

**Reachability.** The parser is invoked on any structured‑address header value on the normal send path (`MimeNode.setHeader('To'/'Cc'/'Bcc'/'From'/'Reply-To', value)` → `_parseAddresses` → `addressparser`, and `getEnvelope()`), so a single `transport.sendMail({ to: <crafted string> })` triggers it. It is also reached directly through the **exported** `require('nodemailer/lib/addressparser')`, which many applications call to validate or display user‑supplied recipient lists. Confirmed via the public API: `setHeader('To', 'a@b.com,'.repeat(80000))` + `getEnvelope()` blocks for ~3.9 s.

**Suggested fix:** accumulate in place instead of rebuilding the array each iteration, e.g. `parsedAddresses.push.apply(parsedAddresses, handled);` (or `for (const h of handled) parsedAddresses.push(h);`). Optionally cap the number of addresses / input length before parsing.

### PoC

Environment: Node.js ≥ 18 and the published `nodemailer@9.0.6`. No transport, network, or configuration required — the cost is in parsing.

`poc-dos.js`:
```js
'use strict';
const addressparser = require('nodemailer/lib/addressparser');

console.log('addresses | input size | parse time');
for (const n of [25000, 50000, 100000, 200000]) {
  const payload = 'a@b.com,'.repeat(n);        // n valid, comma-separated recipients
  const t0 = process.hrtime.bigint();
  addressparser(payload);                       // blocks synchronously
  const ms = Number(process.hrtime.bigint() - t0) / 1e6;
  console.log(String(n).padStart(9) + ' | ' + (payload.length / 1048576).toFixed(2) + ' MB   | ' + ms.toFixed(0).padStart(7) + ' ms');
}
```

Run:
```
npm init -y && npm install nodemailer@9.0.6
node poc-dos.js
```

Actual output (nodemailer 9.0.6):
```
addresses | input size | parse time
    25000 | 0.19 MB   |     381 ms
    50000 | 0.38 MB   |    1435 ms
   100000 | 0.76 MB   |    7949 ms
   200000 | 1.53 MB   |   25154 ms
```

Equivalent trigger through the normal send API (freezes the event loop):
```js
const nodemailer = require('nodemailer');
nodemailer.createTransport({ jsonTransport: true })
  .sendMail({ from: 'a@b.com', to: 'a@b.com,'.repeat(150000), subject: 'x', text: 'y' });
// ~15+ seconds of 100% CPU inside addressparser before anything is sent
```

### Impact

* **Who is impacted:** any service that runs Nodemailer (or the standalone `nodemailer/lib/addressparser`) on an address value that can be influenced by an untrusted party — a recipient field in a "send email / invite / share" feature, a `Reply‑To`/`From` derived from user input, a contact‑import or mailing‑list parser, or any endpoint that validates addresses with `addressparser`. No authentication, special option, or particular receiver is needed.

## Patched in 9.1.0

Three separate quadratic paths were fixed, not one:

* `addressparser` rebuilt its accumulator with `concat()` on every address ([9116da9](https://github.com/nodemailer/nodemailer/commit/9116da9)).
* The display-name merge loop directly below spliced each fragment out of the array, the same shape reached through `'a, b <c@d.com>,'.repeat(n)` (same commit).
* `MimeNode#_convertAddresses` checked recipient uniqueness with a linear scan per address ([7cc38af](https://github.com/nodemailer/nodemailer/commit/7cc38af), refined in [34da642](https://github.com/nodemailer/nodemailer/commit/34da642)). This was the most severe of the three and the reported proof of concept did not reach it: `'a@b.com,'.repeat(n)` is one address repeated, which dedupes to a single envelope entry. A list of *distinct* recipients cost O(n^2) here, taking ~35s for 100k even after `addressparser` was fixed.

Fixed alongside: `[].concat.apply` in `_parseAddresses` threw `RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded` past roughly 124k recipients, with no crafted input needed ([83b8c48](https://github.com/nodemailer/nodemailer/commit/83b8c48)).

Parsing 200k addresses now takes ~80ms instead of ~25s, and every path scales linearly. A new `maxRecipients` option (default 100000) throws rather than truncating, as a backstop.

Vulnerabilities.Title: Nodemailer: Quadratic backtracking in the addressparser free-text fallback allows remote denial of service
Vulnerabilities.Description:
### Summary

When `addressparser` finds no address by its strict reading, it falls back to pulling one out of the free text with `/\s*\b[^@\s]+@[^\s]+\b\s*/`. That pattern backtracks quadratically: `[^@\s]+` is retried from every offset and rescans the run to the next `@` each time. A single header value holding a long whitespace-free run with no usable `@` blocks the Node.js event loop for tens of seconds.

It is cheaper to exploit than GHSA-prgh-xp8r-p3m5: 273KB is enough for ~43s, where the comment-joined shape needed ~1.5MB for ~10s.

### Details

The fallback in `src/addressparser/index.ts` ran the pattern as a search. `[^@\s]+` crosses neither whitespace nor `@`, so from each start offset it scans forward to the next `@` or to the end of the run and then fails, and the engine simply advances one character and repeats. Three shapes make every offset fail:

- the run holds no `@` at all
- the only `@` has nothing after it
- the only `@` has nothing before it

A fourth reaches it with a valid address present but placed past a long run, so the long run is walked before the match is found.

### PoC

```js
const addressparser = require('nodemailer/lib/addressparser');
const s = Date.now();
addressparser(' >' + '>[x][x]'.repeat(40000)); // 273KB
console.log(Date.now() - s, 'ms'); // ~43000 ms, blocking
```

Measured on 10.0.5:

| Value | Parse time |
| --- | --- |
| `'[x]'.repeat(40000)` (117KB) | 9.0 s |
| `'[x]'.repeat(40000) + '@'` (117KB) | 8.9 s |
| `'@' + '[x]'.repeat(40000)` (117KB) | 8.8 s |
| `' >' + '>[x][x]'.repeat(40000)` (273KB) | 42.9 s |

### Impact

Algorithmic-complexity denial of service. Node is single threaded, so the block stalls the whole process. Reachable without authentication anywhere inbound header values are handed to this parser, mailparser being the notable case, and reachable from application input wherever a user-supplied string is used as a message address, since `mime-node` parses `to`, `from` and `cc` when composing.

### Patch

The search is replaced by a single linear pass that finds the one offset the pattern can match at, which is then applied there with a sticky regex. Match results are unchanged, verified against the previous implementation over 3.4 million random strings comparing both the match offset and the matched text, plus 800k full-parse comparisons.

Found while validating the report in GHSA-prgh-xp8r-p3m5, not reported externally.
